reason: The sources provide over a dozen robust, multi-site claims detailing the hexagon's discovery, massive scale, lab recreation, and seasonal color shifts.
story: In 1981, NASA's Voyager probes snapped tantalizing views of Saturn's north pole, revealing something that looked impossible: a giant, nearly perfect hexagon carved into the clouds. Measuring over 20,000 miles wide—large enough to swallow two Earths—this six-sided jet stream whips eastward at over 200 miles per hour, surrounding a violent central polar hurricane. When the Cassini orbiter arrived decades later, it confirmed the geometric vortex was still spinning, locked tightly with Saturn's internal rotation period of 10 hours and 39 minutes. Over its multi-year mission, Cassini even watched the hexagon shift in color from deep blue to golden haze as solar radiation reacted with atmospheric methane during the long Saturnian summer. Laboratory physicists eventually cracked the geometry: spinning fluid in circular tanks naturally buckles into stable polygons when sharp speed gradients clash, proving that fluid physics can sculpt pure geometry out of atmospheric chaos.
angle: A six-sided jet stream wider than two Earths has remained locked at Saturn's north pole for decades, and physicists can recreate the exact geometric storm in a simple spinning tank of water.

claims.claim: Saturn's north pole is circled by a persistent, roughly symmetrical six-sided hexagonal jet stream.
The hexagonal pattern was first spotted in images sent back by the Voyager flybys in 1980 and 1981.
David Godfrey identified the hexagonal feature after analyzing the Voyager flyby data.
The entire hexagonal pattern spans roughly 20,000 miles across, making it more than twice the width of Earth.
Each straight side of the hexagon is longer than the entire diameter of Earth.
The perimeter jet stream moves at speeds of approximately 200 miles per hour (320 km/h).
The hexagon rotates with a period of roughly 10 hours and 39 minutes, matching the rotation of Saturn's interior.
The center of the hexagon encloses a circular polar hurricane-like vortex marking Saturn's north pole.
Saturn's south pole does not possess a hexagonal jet stream.
When Cassini reached Saturn in 2004, the north pole was in winter darkness, requiring initial observations in thermal infrared.
Between winter and summer solstice, the hexagon visibly shifted from a bluish tone to a golden-yellow hue.
The seasonal color shift is driven by increased sunlight generating a photochemical hydrocarbon haze from methane.
The hexagon extends hundreds of kilometers above the cloud tops into Saturn's stratosphere.
Saturn takes about 29 to 30 Earth years to orbit the Sun, meaning each season lasts more than seven Earth years.
Scientists recreated the hexagonal flow pattern in laboratory experiments using rotating cylindrical tanks with fluid speed gradients.
In laboratory fluid tanks, varying the rotation speeds also produces other regular polygons like triangles, squares, and octagons.
Cassini performed 22 dives between the planet and its rings during its Grand Finale before plunging into the atmosphere on September 15, 2017.
Cassini was deliberately plunged into Saturn to prevent Earth microbes from contaminating potentially habitable moons.

disputed: Side length measurements: S1 cites approximately 14,500 km (9,000 miles), while S5 and S7 cite approximately 13,800 km (8,600 miles). Scripts should state 'around 14,000 kilometers' or 'longer than Earth's diameter'.
Jet wind speeds: S1, S4, and S7 state wind speeds around 200 mph (320 km/h), whereas S2 states about 300 mph (500 km/h). Scripts should qualify perimeter wind speeds as exceeding 200 to 300 mph.
Discovery date of the pattern: S1 gives 1987 as Godfrey's discovery year, while S6 and S7 cite his published paper in 1988. Attribute simply as 'discovered in the late 1980s from Voyager images'.

Depth of the mechanism: Sources dispute whether the hexagon is a shallow atmospheric wave (S4, S6) or a deep-rooted convective jet extending thousands of kilometers into the interior (S2, S6). Frame this as an ongoing scientific debate.
